item.title: Public broadcasters to be merged into four “houses” from 2029
item.description:
Public broadcasters to be merged into four “houses” from 2029

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet has published its plan to reform the Dutch public broadcasting system, which will replace the current 11 broadcasting organisations with four “broadcasting houses” from 2029.

News broadcaster NOS and educational broadcaster NTR will also merge under the NOS name, and no new broadcasters will be allowed to join the system, media minister Rianne Letschert told parliament on Friday, NOS reported.

The plan was first drawn up last year and was included in the coalition agreement and is open to public consultation.

Current system
There are currently 11 public broadcasting organisations under the umbrella of public broadcasting body NPO: AVROTROS, BNNVARA, EO, Human, KRO-NCRV, Max, Ongehoord Nederland (ON), PowNed, VPRO, WNL and Zwart.

Each has its own political, religious or social focus and together they make programmes for three national television channels and five radio stations.

To join, a group must sign up at least 50,000 paying members, which earns it a provisional licence for five years. To keep a permanent place it needs 100,000 members.

A broadcaster can lose its licence if the media regulator sanctions it twice in five years, if it no longer meets the legal requirements, or if the NPO says it refuses to cooperate with the others. These are the three grounds Letschert used last week when she said she would withdraw the licence of far-right broadcaster ON.

Under the new plan, the membership requirement is scrapped and broadcasters will no longer be able to join the system or be thrown out, although the regulator will still be able to act against wrongdoing.

Four houses
Which broadcasters go into which house has not been decided yet, but the broadcasters have already said who they want to work with: KRO-NCRV, Max and WNL; EO, VPRO and Human; AVROTROS and PowNed; and BNNVARA and Zwart.

Zwart, set up by rapper Akwasi to bring more diversity to television, has been broadcasting on a provisional licence since 2022 but still has to win a permanent one before it can join a house.

The houses can keep their old names or choose new ones, and will have more say over their own programming as the NPO’s coordinating role shrinks.

Letschert said the current system has too many boards and too much internal competition. “With less administrative bustle and more shared responsibility, the public broadcaster can focus on making good programmes, strong journalism and digital innovation,” she said.

The media regulator, the Commissariaat voor de Media, has criticised the plan, saying it gives broadcasters too few clear rules and relies too much on self-regulation.

The draft law goes next to the Council of State (Raad van State), the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, and then to parliament and the senate. The cabinet wants the new system to start in 2029.

item.title: FNV union demands 5.5% pay rises to tackle high inflation
item.description:
FNV union demands 5.5% pay rises to tackle high inflation

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Trade unions are demanding pay rises of up 5.5% in next year’s pay round to offset the impact of high inflation.

The FNV, the Netherlands’ largest labour union, published its demands on Monday as part of the regular build-up to the opening of parliament and Budget Day this week.

The FNV says it will press for a 5.5% increase in basic pay during collective bargaining negotiations and a flat payment of €80 a month for all workers to give an extra boost to low earners.

Inflation is currently 3.3%, having risen in August, according to the government statistics agency CBS.

“We see that inflation is rising and is still well above the average while productivity is rising, companies are making big profits and the labour market remains tight,” Jacqie van Stigt, the union’s interim collective bargaining co-ordinator said.

The CNV, another of the major unions, said last week it would be seeking pay rises of between 3% and 5.5% next year as well as an increase in the travel allowance to 25 cents per kilometre, after the government raised the maximum tax-free amount from July 1.

AI concerns

The FNV also said it wanted to draw up stricter rules to ensure employees were consulted on the use of AI in the workplace.

The union is concerned that using machine-generated text is leading to more pressure on workers and giving companies an excuse to cut jobs.

The FNV also announced that cleaning staff have begun a week-long strike to protest against the pay deal struck between employers and the CNV union, which 80% of FNV members have rejected.

Staff at Schiphol airport and railway stations will take part in the strike. The union wants the employers to go back to the table and discuss their demands, which include not cutting pay for sick employees and paying hotel cleaners equal rates.

“We will continue until the pay negotiations are reopened and our cleaners are actually listened to,” said union spokeswoman Carolien Lambers.

item.title: The 2026 budget: what we know and what has been leaked so far
item.description:
The 2026 budget: what we know and what has been leaked so far

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

As happens every year, large parts of the government’s spending plans have been leaked to the Dutch press. Here is a summary of what the various papers are reporting is being planned:

Government and local government finances

  • The government plans to cut €400 million from spending on its own operations, with the aim of a structural reduction of €1 billion from 2030.
  • In particular, the government plans to reduce support functions and ensure external hires account for no more than 10% of the workforce.
  • The local authorities fund will rise marginally to just under €50 billion, or €2,741 per resident.
  • However, local authorities will not be compensated for spending on youth social work and €1 billion will be cut from the budget for home helps.

Taxes

  • Spending power will fall marginally for all but pensioners and low-income households.
  • Plans to reform the Box 3 asset tax system are due in spring 2027.
  • Income tax rates will go down by 0.06 percentage points in the first and second tax bands.
  • The arbeidskorting – a tax break for people in work – will rise slightly.
  • Employers will no longer be able to give workers a 20% discount tax free on the company’s own products.
  • Staff outings and Christmas boxes will no longer be tax free.
  • The startersaftrek – a discount for the newly self-employed – will be scrapped although it is not yet clear when.
  • BTW on plants, flowers and trips by balloon will rise from 9% to 21%.
  • Excise duty on alcohol will rise in line with inflation.

Benefits

  • Cuts to slash the period for claiming unemployment benefit from two to one year have been delayed until 2029.
  • A planned faster increase in the state pension age will not go ahead.
  • A lower maximum for payouts to pregnant women and people on invalidity benefit will not go ahead.

Travel and transport

  • A 10 cent reduction in the price of diesel will be phased out from 2028 not 2027.
  • Tax on long-distance flights is being set at €59 instead of €70 to ensure Schiphol is not more expensive than German airports.

Healthcare

  • A planned increase in the health insurance own risk payment of €60 has been scrapped. It will still rise from €385 to €400 in line with inflation.
  • €100 million is being allocated to ensure 60 to 69-year-olds can be vaccinated against shingles. The over 70s must pick up the bill themselves.
  • The government expects health insurance premiums will rise by €12 a month – although health insurance companies decide their own rates.

Housing and infrastructure

  • €940 million will be allocated to boost major residential developments in terms of facilities and green spaces.
  • €630 million will go to specialised housing for the elderly.
  • Housing corporations will get a €425 million tax cut, allowing them to borrow an extra €6 billion to build social housing.
  • Private investors will be able to claim up to €10,000 for every mid-market rental home they build, from a budget of €500 million running from 2029 to 2033.
  • €1.5 billion has been allocated for road and bridge repairs.
  • €300 million will be invested annually in improving transport links to new residential developments.

Education and research

  • Education will get €668 million extra, largely reversing cuts to higher education imposed by the previous government.
  • There will be more investment in trade schools and in scientific research.
  • Funding is being set aside for the development of a national super computer and an Einstein telescope R&D centre.
  • The basic grant for students living away from home will rise by €50 from 2028.
  • €346 million will go to additional training for teachers from 2028.
  • More money will be allocated to help people shift into teaching from other professions.

Climate

  • Money will be allocated to help farmers who want to invest in making their businesses more sustainable and climate-friendly.
  • €1.3 billion is being allocated to store carbon dioxide in empty gas fields under the North Sea.

Asylum and migration

  • The government says spending on refugees will reach €8 billion this year but go down to €5 billion by 2031 because of EU and other measures.
  • Local authorities which have not set up their own permanent refugee centres will be placed on a blacklist.
  • €22 million will be invested in setting up refugee centres outside the EU in 2027.
  • More money will be put into dealing with refugees who commit crimes and in secure accommodation for them.

Royals

  • Spending on staff etc. will rise from €60.8 million to €62.1 million in 2027.
  • The king, queen and princess Amalia will have combined income of €2.7 million this year, but Amalia will not claim hers while she is studying.
  • The royals’ income rises in line with civil servant pay, which is 0.3% this year.

Other

  • €600 million extra will go to defence in 2027, taking the total to almost €29 billion, including €3.1 billion in military support for Ukraine.
  • The development aid budget will rise by €400 million a year for the next three years, on top of the extra money agreed in June to win senate support and the partial reversal of the Schoof cabinet’s €2.4 billion cuts.
  • The Netherlands will not hit the OECD target of 0.7% of GDP on aid spending.
  • The government will introduce a “sport pass” for 12 to 23-year-olds of €100 to €300 to be invested in sports.

Sources: Telegraaf, NRC, NOS, RTL and Volkskrant

item.title: Passengers evacuated after train hits lorry on level crossing
item.description:
Passengers evacuated after train hits lorry on level crossing

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Around 150 passengers have been evacuated from a train after it collided with a lorry on a level crossing in Gelderland.

Two people on the train and the lorry driver suffered minor injuries in the collision on Horsterweg, Elmelo, train operator NS said.

The Sprinter train was heading towards Harderwijk when the crash happened just after 10am on Monday. The passengers were escorted to the station before buses were arranged to take them to their destinations.

The lorry was transporting concrete blocks on a low loader. NS said the clean-up operation would take several hours and all trains between Amersfoort and Zwolle have been cancelled for the rest of the day. Replacement buses are running between Putten and Nunspeet.

Police said the lorry driver was taken to hospital for treatment. The investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing.

item.title: Brainwash: Anatomy of a Dutch language course
item.description:
Partner content

Brainwash: Anatomy of a Dutch language course

September 14, 2026

Ready to start speaking Dutch? The Dutch Brainwash school, which sponsored this piece, invited DutchNews’ Lauren Comiteau to visit a class.

On the sweltering August day I visit Albert Both’s Brainwash class on the Keizersgracht in the heart of the Jordaan, you can hear the laughter before you even enter the room.

During this last class of Both’s current one-week intensive Dutch language course, eight students – Both’s maximum per course – sit around a huge white table that takes up most of the room. Amidst the organised chaos are stuffed animals, books and games, all props to help the students learn Dutch, or as Albert says, “they’re part of the story to get people talking”.

Armed with fans, water bottles and notebooks full of the handouts they’ve been given throughout the week, all eyes are on Both, who is working a whiteboard via his computer and talking about the past tense.

“It’s the first thing people teach you when you’re learning Dutch,” says Both, “but it’s like giving cauliflower to a baby. The past tense is akin to opening Pandora’s box. If I show it too soon, it will be pure quicksand.”

Instead, after a week of talking and learning, Both gets to the past tense, telling his students the secret to faking it until they make it.

“The trick is you can use the present tense to talk about the past,” he says. You do that, he continues, by saying one sentence in the past tense, pausing, and then continuing in the present tense. “If you do it with elegance and grace, no one knows you’re cheating. I’ve been doing it for a very long time.”

Informal, fun and funny

“I’ve done six different types of courses trying to learn Dutch,” says American independent researcher Lauren Vargas (45), who currently lives in Leiden. “This is the first one where I’ve learned more in seven days than I have in six years.”

She chalks that up to Albert’s teaching style, a far cry, she says, from her other classes where teachers focused too much on structure without theory and application. “Here, you build up to better understand the mechanics, and we’re encouraged to be playful with the language, to make mistakes, to accept that we can actually speak more and understand more than we think we do.”

They can do that because of the informal atmosphere Albert has honed over the years. “We sit around a table like a group of friends,” he says. “My students inspire each other to learn. We create a safe and fun atmosphere, as compared to their past traumatic experiences learning Dutch, which were often impersonal and had students sitting there like they were in a factory.”

The casual conversations – which focus on anything the students want, including the sex toy a sex worker once brought in or a headlining murder investigation that led to a murder-themed discussion – uniquely bind the students. The stuffed Jesus toy is to stimulate conversations about religion.

“That really helped break the ice and get us more comfortable with each other,” says student Jamie Tipelto. “Then we’re able to be more open and freer about speaking and making mistakes. It’s a safe space.”

Fellow student Jesse Corcoran (47), an American researcher at UMC Utecht, who’s lived in the Netherlands for only four months, ditched her more structured and academic Dutch class and followed her husband into Albert’s Brainwash.

“My old class always filled me with anxiety because there wasn’t a lot of ice-breaking, and I wasn’t really comfortable with the people that I was in class with,” she says. “Here, from the first day, the ice is broken, and then you’re more comfortable making mistakes and trying new things.”

“It’s definitely given me more confidence to speak to my neighbours. And that’s a big thing for my husband and I because we want to integrate and become part of the culture. So getting that courage and that confidence to speak to Dutch people is paramount.”

65,000 mistakes

Even for those who have been in the Netherlands longer, like Romanian product manager Sudi (46), who has lived here for 15 years, Albert’s class was a gamechanger.

“I’d taken inburgering classes before, but they created a fear in me of making mistakes,” she says. “Coming to this course made a big difference, because we signed a contract to make 65,000 mistakes. I think I’ve made 30,000, so I still have 30,000 to go!”

Sudi had been following Albert on social media and related to his postings that seemed to echo her situation – getting over the speaking-Dutch hump.

“Now, in the process of making my mistake quota, I’m more confident speaking Dutch and being part of the community. It was a great choice.”

For American Shemby Nagel, who took the course with her friend Lauren Vargas, Albert’s class gave her an unexpected energy boost. “With every language course I’ve tried to take in the past, after about an hour or two, your energy level just goes down. You tank and you’re just dreading coming in the next day. You don’t have time or energy for homework,” she says.

“This is the very first language class – or any class – I’ve taken where my energy level has just gone up and up and up. So by the time I finish, Lauren and I travel back to Leiden and continually work on what we learned in class. And when I get home, I’ll have conversations with my partner and my daughter in Dutch, which I never would have done before.”

Ongelooflijk!

“We have an amazing time together,” says Sandra from Mexico, a procurement manager who has lived in the Netherlands for 10 years.

Albert is legendary among those looking to learn Dutch, and she liked the reviews that talked about his jokes and non-traditional way of teaching. She made the daily commute from Rotterdam, “feeling so happy to be here and excited that he broke through my fear of speaking”.

At the same time, she says his class “opened her ears” to listening to Dutch on the streets, something she had previously avoided because she didn’t understand the language. “That’s how I found my new favourite word: ongelooflijk (unbelievable)!”

Only the beginning

As class winds down, Albert reminds his students one last time to keep on talking. “You can do more than you think,” he tells them. “You must! At some point, you must just say it, even if you think it’s wrong. That’s the reality.”

One by one, the students go around the table saying, “Ik spreek Nederlands,” or “I speak Dutch”.

Albert hands them their diplomas, and then they gather their belongings and head out to a local café for a well-earned drink.

“Het is niet het einde, maar het begin,” he tells them. “It is not the end, but the beginning.”

For anyone looking for a Dutch refresher class, struggling with stalled motivation or wanting to start truly speaking Dutch, Both’s class has proven invaluable. You can sign up here for the next Dutch Brainwash!

item.title: Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery
item.description:
Scientists develop “tickle robot” to solve touching mystery

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Researchers in Nijmegen have set up a laboratory to try to answer one of the oldest questions known to science: why are people ticklish?

Aristotle, Erasmus, Galileo and Darwin all tried to put their finger on the purpose of tickling, or gargalesis to use its scientific name, without finding a definitive reason.

Now two researchers at Radboud University in Nijmegen are using robots and sensors to try to shed more light on the phenomenon.

Tickling exists across cultures and throughout history, but with few variations and little difference between men and women, indicating that it has its roots in biology. Tickling has been observed in other primates such as bonobos and chimpanzees.

Ziliang Xiong and Konstantina Kilteni have set up their lab in a windowless basement in the Maria Montessori building, an environment stripped of any other stimuli that could make their test subjects laugh.

The robot uses a metal pin to simulate tickling, with settings that can be adjusted to measure the effect of different types of contact from gentle stroking to prodding. The participants wear a cap equipped with electrodes that measure their brain responses.

Families and partners

The researchers also asked the 448 subjects to fill in surveys about how they experienced tickling, which revealed strong similiarities.

Most tickling is by adults on children, usually within families, or between siblings. Partners and friends also tickle each other, but this is less common.

Most respondents said they reacted to tickling by laughing, squirming or trying to turn away. The vast majority named the same body parts as most susceptible to tickling: the sides, armpits, belly and the soles of the feet.

The researchers noted that while tickling is associated with play and laughter, many people find it unpleasant and it can quickly become overwhelming. The Nazis even used it as a torture method.

There are indications that people diagnosed with autism are more sensitive to tickling and that ticklish people may even live longer.

Other theories suggest a link between tickling and sexual stimulation, given that couples often tickle each other and it tends to be directed at body parts that are rarely exposed.

Thin skinned

Darwin speculated that tickling felt uncomfortable because it involved touching parts of the body that are unused to being touch, while Aristotle believed it worked on places where the skin is thinner.

But the researchers in Nijmegen said none of the theories provided a complete answer to the reasons why people are sensitive to tickling. “You rarely get touched on your back, but the back is pretty resistant to tickling,” Xiong pointed out.

item.title: Notorious fugitive Dutch arms dealer dies in South Africa
item.description:
Notorious fugitive Dutch arms dealer dies in South Africa

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A timber merchant turned arms dealer, one of the Netherlands’ most infamous international fugitives, has died peacefully in South Africa after evading justice for years.

Guus Kouwenhoven, who facilitated weapons shipments to the Liberian dictator Charles Taylor in the early 2000s, was sentenced in absentia to 19 years for illegal arms smuggling and complicity in war crimes in 2017.

Despite being arrested in Cape Town, he was released on bail and avoided extradition, living a life of luxury, until his death last week.

Taylor, who was himself given a 50-year prison sentence in The Hague for crimes against humanity, waged civil wars in Liberia until 2003 that killed over 150,000 people. Kouwenhoven’s dealings with him were seen as instrumental to the fighting, which was notorious for its brutality and widespread use of child soldiers.

The Liberian press described Kouwenhoven as a reminder of the country’s violent past, referring to “blood timber”, and asked how someone could get away with turning the timber trade into a currency for war.

So far nothing has been said by Dutch justice minister David van Weel, despite the scale and notoriety of the case. Efforts to have him extradited were complicated and delayed even after South Africa revoked his visa, and his exuberant lifestyle reportedly went unhindered.

Given the recent efforts by Van Weel to push for Sierra Leone to extradite fugitive drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers – even by asking the EU to cut off development aid to the country until it hands him over – Kouwenhoven seems to have escaped proportional scrutiny in his final years, a Volkskrant column argued.

item.title: Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site
item.description:
Woman arrested after trying to hire hitman on dark web scam site

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A woman has been arrested for allegedly trying to recruit a hitman on the dark web to kill her ex-husband.

Police confirmed that the 45-year-old woman was arrested in Rotterdam at the weekend for being “involved” in organising a contract killing after the case came to light during an investigation by RTL Nieuws.

The website turned out to be a scam that advertised non-existent “contract killing” services and the attack was never carried out, despite the client transferring US$1,400 (€1,200) in bitcoins as a downpayment.

The man, who was given the cover name of Jerom by RTL, told the broadcaster he was “incredibly relieved that the police have identified a suspect”

The client instructed the website “burn him alive and make sure he doesn’t survive.” When told that the attack would cost $9,000, they replied: “OK, how much does it cost to cut off his arms and legs or shoot him?”

Elderly mother

The instructions included Jerom’s home address, a recent photograph and information about the house, including the alarm system and the fact that his elderly mother lived with him.

“The only demand is that he has to die. I don’t care what happens to the mother,” the client wrote.

Police said arranging the killing was still a crime even though the hitman did not exist. They did not confirm if the request had come directly from the businessman’s ex-wife.

In 2021 a man from The Hague was given an eight-year jail sentence for trying to arrange a murder on the same website. A judge said he had acted “coldly and clinically” in instructing the killing and could take no credit for the fact that the victim was still alive.

item.title: Jetten braced for more tough negotiations to pass budget bill
item.description:
Jetten braced for more tough negotiations to pass budget bill

September 14, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prinsjesdag, the first day of the Dutch parliamentary year, should be a high point in the finance minister’s calendar, when he or she sets down the next year’s budget plans in a neat pile and unties the ribbons.

This year, however, Eelco Heinen looks more like a man whose papers have been blown around in a gale, forcing him to scramble around to recover them and tie them up with loose bits of string.

Heinen and Rob Jetten’s hopes of doing a deal with opposition parties before Budget Day on September 15 have been dashed, meaning the minority coalition will now have to find the votes as the bills pass through parliament.

Jetten wanted to agree a package of measures with opposition parties on both left and right, to avoid the “yo-yo politics” that hamstrung his predecessor as prime minister, Dick Schoof.

The talks broke down partly because both sides demanded a high price, but also because the coalition parties were split on what concessions to make.

The outcome is a fudge that appeals to nobody’s taste. And as Jetten has said, the budget that will be presented to parliament next Tuesday is “not the end”. Without an advance deal, the minority coalition will have to keep negotiating to find the 10 seats it needs in the lower house and 16 in the senate.

Spending cuts delayed

Heinen’s party, the right-wing liberal VVD, has had to climb down on its insistence that the €6.5 billion of cuts to welfare spending outlined in the coalition agreement were non-negotiable.

The left-wing opposition party Pro, formerly the alliance of GroenLinks-PvdA, had campaigned to abandon the welfare cuts altogether, supported by the trade unions, who called a one-day nationwide transport workers’ strike last week.

The government wanted to reduce the maximum term for unemployment pay from two years to one, phase out the incapacity benefit IVA and reduce the maximum payment for a range of other benefits, including sick pay and maternity leave, by 20%.

But most of the measures have been postponed by a year rather than cancelled, prompting Pro leader Jesse Klaver to comment that the revised budget was “maybe worse than the original plans”. The unions have said the strikes will continue until the cuts are scrapped.

Cost of living

Klaver told a party congress at the weekend that his party was willing to discuss reforming the WIA incapacity benefit rules, but only if the cuts were taken off the table.

“Pro was founded to combat inequality and strengthen the welfare state,” he said. “You can’t ask us to help you take it apart.”

The left-wing opposition had already forced the cabinet to back down on a proposal to cut the pensions bill by raising the retirement age in step with life expectancy, rather than by eight months for every extra year, which would have saved €2.8 billion a year.

On the right, parties such as JA21 have pressed for the cabinet to make further savings on social security to fund tax cuts across the board and offset the rising cost of living. Inflation is running at 3.3%, driven by soaring fuel and energy prices.

The cabinet has agreed to extend the discount on fuel duty into next year to provide relief for motorists who are paying the highest petrol and diesel prices in Europe.

The cabinet has also allocated €1.7 million to offsetting rising living costs, a response to recent figures from the economic planning bureau CPB that projected a 0.3% drop in spending power next year.

Top earners

With the spending cuts watered down, the government found the money by raising an extra €750 million in income tax on high earners, as well as a small increase in the domestic water levy, according to documents leaked to the commercial broadcaster RTL.

Despite the cash injection, the graphics produced by the finance ministry show that most income groups will still experience a drop in spending power and those who benefit will be pensioners and people on the lowest incomes.

The Telegraaf reported last week that the finance ministry expects the average premium for universal healthcare to go up by €120 a year to €2,028.

The plan to increase the health insurance deductible, or excess, by €60 is also being delayed by a year. It will still rise with inflation for the first time in a decade, so patients will pay €395 up front for medical treatment, €10 more than this year.

Extended negotiation

Part of the reason the negotiations ran into difficulty is that Jetten and Heinen effectively ran parallel talks, with the prime minister trying to agree the political terms while Heinen concentrated on balancing the books.

The VVD finance minister reportedly “shocked” his coalition partners when he produced a draft document that was weighted heavily in favour of right-wing parties such as JA21 and the hardline Protestant SGP, but was unpalatable to the more centrist D66 and CDA, who wanted to bring Pro on board.

After a weekend of emergency talks within the coalition, a revised budget was agreed on Monday, August 31 – the last possible deadline for the draft to be sent to the Council of State for analysis, which is a legal requirement.

At first glance, the revised deal looks like a setback for the VVD, which campaigned during last year’s election and the coalition negotiations that followed on a platform of keeping Pro out of cabinet and marginalising its influence.

With the cabinet lacking a majority in parliament, Pro has a pivotal role as the largest opposition party. Its 20 seats in the Tweede Kamer would give the coalition parties a comfortable majority, while in the upper house the cabinet plus Pro are just two seats short.

Jetten is aware, however, that too many concessions to Pro will risk the balance within his coalition. At some point, Jesse Klaver’s party will have to settle on the welfare cuts, which could test his alliance with the trade unions.

BBB blockers

Another potential stumbling block is the farmers’ party BBB, which was frozen out of the talks because it refused to support the cabinet’s measures to cut nitrogen pollution, which all three coalition parties stand resolutely behind.

The BBB could form a blocking minority in the Senate, where they have 11 seats, and have already threatened to cause trouble over the cabinet’s plans to reform the asset tax system.

The right-wing opposition is larger but disjointed, with Geert Wilders’ PVV and Forum voor Democratie refusing to negotiate in the hope that they can force early elections.

The result is that while parliament has an in-built right-wing majority, it is the left who have had the upper hand in the negotiations so far.

As the budget bill goes through parliament, Rob Jetten faces the double-headed challenge of finding the votes he needs from the opposition while holding his battered coalition together.

item.title: Government bodies collaborate to scrap their penalty payments
item.description:
Government bodies collaborate to scrap their penalty payments

September 14, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Government organisations have been working together to get the financial penalties they owe for missing their deadlines scrapped, an investigation by newspaper Trouw has found.

Officials at the immigration service IND, the benefits agency UWV and the tax office’s benefits arm have been in communication about whether they can push for a complete legal change, freeing them from any fines for failure to comply with their duties.

Internal emails and memos obtained via freedom of information requests show an IND adviser writing to a counterpart at the tax office last year saying they’re looking into abolishing penalties altogether and wants to “see whether abolition for the whole of administrative law is possible”.

Since 2009, anyone whose application for a permit, benefit or allowance is not decided within the legal deadline can be entitled to remedial payments.

The relevant agency is first put on notice, and then if it still fails to decide within two weeks, it owes a daily penalty, rising to a maximum of €1,442, and the applicant can go to court, where a judge can impose an even higher one.

The IND is by far the biggest payer. It paid out nearly €100 million in the first half of this year, almost all of it on asylum cases. Some individual claimants received over €100,000. The agencies say they cannot meet their deadlines because of staff shortages and rising caseloads.

Immigration applicants have already lost the right to automatic penalty payments under an earlier law. In March, MPs from the SGP, ChristenUnie, JA21 and VVD voted to scrap court-imposed ones too, for all immigration cases including residence permits.

The Senate is expected to debate it on September 22, broadcaster NOS reported. Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has said he wants the same for the UWV.
Asked about the emails, an IND spokesperson told Trouw the service is in contact with agencies facing “the same problems” and that “experiences are exchanged”.
